data.title: The River’s Next Course
data.text:
The river took the Upper Vell dam, the first chalet in the village, and the fjord chapel. The village lift remains, and Tomas Lind’s chalet still stands. His letter asks for a new stake line, higher up, where the ice still is. I have put that beside Anna Sorel’s handover note: the dam was sized for the lake as surveyed, and she warned it would not hold a larger one.

You came down at 109 tonnes, through five waterfalls, and reached the coast. Earlier, the field cabin above the third falls was gone; later, No. 14 and the Pells’ house, then Riverside dam. The bolted stone and the Cut bridge were left standing on their days. I have kept those pages together, though they were made in different years.

Calder expanded the plant; the council deferred Sorel’s flood works; the Ministry called Riverside dam satisfactory without a visit. Households already stretched voted down a levy. Far beyond the valley, the largest emitters kept burning. The weight was not shared evenly, and the valley’s choices decided what the thaw met.

I am Mara Vey. The Water Board has now funded a second crossing; the Ministry has announced spillway upgrades. Tomas’s stake line is still a question with a place to be drilled. You cannot undo the river behind you. You can still decide where it goes next.

data.title: The Stake Line
data.text:
The Upper Vell dam went, and the lake came down the route Anna Sorel had drawn in red. You crossed five waterfalls; your mass peaked at 109 tonnes. The fjord chapel was destroyed. The village lift and Tomas Lind’s chalet remained intact.

Earlier, the field cabin above the third falls was lost. Its notebooks had already been given away. I am Mara Vey. I have set that memory beside Tomas’s letter, where he asks someone to drill a new stake line higher up, where the ice still is. The request is not a stake in the ground.

In 2017, the town voted on a yearly household charge for a flood wall and a higher dam spillway. More voted no than yes. The wall was eventually built with national money, to the old design. In 2025, after national co-funding was withdrawn, the Water Board postponed Kessel’s spillway works. Calder marked relocation deferred and upstream spillway co-funding outside company policy; its Board accepted the risk. The choices were made in different rooms, by people with different shares of what followed.

Tomas’s notebooks are in the archive. The new stake line is still a request.

data.title: The Open Line
data.text:
The route in my boxes begins with Tomas Lind’s measurements. The field cabin went, though its notebooks had already been given away. Later the river took No. 14 Church Lane and the Riverside dam, then the Kessel dam. In Power Valley, it broke the co-op turbine. I keep those papers in separate folders; the consequences did not fall on everyone in the same way.

The decisions are there too. Riverside’s council deferred the spillway works; households voted down a yearly levy, though one spoilt paper said, “I would if I could.” Later, the Ministry withdrew co-funding for Kessel, the Water Board postponed the works, and Calder’s Board accepted the residual risk while relocation stayed deferred. Different rooms, different authority. A blank was left for who would bear it.

In this last descent, the Upper Vell dam gave way and the fjord chapel was destroyed. Tomas Lind’s chalet is still standing. His letter says someone should drill a new stake line higher up, where the ice still is. I have put it here beside the other papers. The line is not drawn yet.

drafts.title: The River’s Next Course
drafts.text:
The river took the Upper Vell dam, the first chalet in the village, and the fjord chapel. The village lift remains, and Tomas Lind’s chalet still stands. His letter asks for a new stake line, higher up, where the ice still is. I have put that beside Anna Sorel’s handover note: the dam was sized for the lake as surveyed, and she warned it would not hold a larger one.

You came down at 109 tonnes, through five waterfalls, and reached the coast. Earlier, the field cabin above the third falls was gone; later, No. 14 and the Pells’ house, then Riverside dam. The bolted stone and the Cut bridge were left standing on their days. I have kept those pages together, though they were made in different years.

Calder expanded the plant; the council deferred Sorel’s flood works; the Ministry called Riverside dam satisfactory without a visit. Households already stretched voted down a levy. Far beyond the valley, the largest emitters kept burning. The weight was not shared evenly, and the valley’s choices decided what the thaw met.

I am Mara Vey. The Water Board has now funded a second crossing; the Ministry has announced spillway upgrades. Tomas’s stake line is still a question with a place to be drilled. You cannot undo the river behind you. You can still decide where it goes next.

drafts.title: The Stake Line
drafts.text:
The Upper Vell dam went, and the lake came down the route Anna Sorel had drawn in red. You crossed five waterfalls; your mass peaked at 109 tonnes. The fjord chapel was destroyed. The village lift and Tomas Lind’s chalet remained intact.

Earlier, the field cabin above the third falls was lost. Its notebooks had already been given away. I am Mara Vey. I have set that memory beside Tomas’s letter, where he asks someone to drill a new stake line higher up, where the ice still is. The request is not a stake in the ground.

In 2017, the town voted on a yearly household charge for a flood wall and a higher dam spillway. More voted no than yes. The wall was eventually built with national money, to the old design. In 2025, after national co-funding was withdrawn, the Water Board postponed Kessel’s spillway works. Calder marked relocation deferred and upstream spillway co-funding outside company policy; its Board accepted the risk. The choices were made in different rooms, by people with different shares of what followed.

Tomas’s notebooks are in the archive. The new stake line is still a request.
